### Chapter 2: Quantity — Investigation 1, the common properties

The chapter on **quantity** (*kamm*) comprises three investigations: its common properties, time, and place. Of its common properties three are distinguished.

**First: divisibility in virtue of itself.** Other things, whether bodies or accidents, are divisible only by means of quantity. Division is used in two senses: **imaginary division**, when we suppose within a thing something distinct from something else; and **actual division**, when the thing is really separated and cut, so that two individual entities arise where previously there was one. Most philosophers define quantity by divisibility, calling it “an accident which admits division in virtue of itself.” What they intend is division in imagination, as will be explained.

**Second: admitting equality and inequality.** Relative to another quantity, a quantity must be either equal, greater, or less. This property follows from the first. Since a quantity comprises imaginary or actual parts, comparison with another quantity requires that the numbers of their parts be equal or unequal. The Imām [al-Rāzī] also relates the admission of division to this property. Since bodies can measure one another without always being equal, they must possess something which intrinsically admits equality and inequality: this is **magnitude** (*miqdār*). Inequality is conceivable only if one quantity contains an equivalent of the other **together with something additional**; hence it must admit division, that is, the supposition of distinct portions.

**Third: including a constituent by which the whole may be numbered**—by repeatedly subtracting or setting off that constituent. This may occur actually, as with **discrete quantity**: four is counted by the unit four times. Or it may occur potentially, as with **continuous quantity**: a year is counted in months, months in days, and a day in hours; a cubit is measured by handbreadths, a handbreadth by fingers, a finger by barleycorn-widths, and the latter by hairs. The Imām states that this third property is suitable for the definition of quantity, unlike the others. As for equality, its definition appears to involve agreement in quantity and so would make a definition of quantity through equality circular. One might reply that equality and inequality are perceived by sense in their subjects, although not as separate objects; as intelligible notions they are grasped by intellect. The proposal could then be to define what is intellectually conceived through what is sensibly encountered.

As for divisibility, the Imām objects that it belongs to continuous quantity and not discrete quantity, so a definition through it would fail to cover all its subjects. I take this to be based on an understanding of “admitting” as the possibility of **acquiring** something not yet actually possessed. Division, however, is already actual in discrete quantity. If “admitting” is understood more generally as the possibility of distinguishing one portion from another in thought, this plainly covers both continuous and discrete quantity. This is why the Imām says that divisibility is an attribute of the continuous rather than the discrete, unless “admitting” is used equivocally.

As for the suggestion in *al-Mawāqif* that the Imām must have intended **separation into actually disconnected parts**, it is a clear mistake. He expressly says at this point that such actual separation cannot befall a magnitude *while it remains numerically the same magnitude*: separation destroys that magnitude and produces **two other magnitudes**. A magnitude does indeed dispose the matter to receive division, but the disposition is not itself necessarily present in the magnitude or preserved when division takes place. In the same way, motion can dispose a body toward natural rest but does not remain together with that rest.

title: Continuous and discrete quantity; geometric magnitude; quantity by derivation
en:
### Continuous and discrete quantity; geometric magnitude; quantity by derivation

**On the words, “And the continuous.”** Another property of quantity is its division into **continuous** and **discrete**, and the further division of the continuous. Either the parts we suppose within a quantity have a **common boundary**, or they do not. In the latter case it is discrete quantity, namely **number** and nothing else. Number in its own right is simply what is composed of units. Other things are numbered only through receiving number as an attribute, inasmuch as their parts receive unity as an attribute. This applies even to spoken discourse, which some have mistakenly imagined to be discrete quantity, as will be explained when letters are discussed.

If the hypothetical parts do share a boundary, the quantity is **continuous**. It is either enduring or permanent in respect of its parts existing together (*qārr al-dhāt*), or it is not. The nonpermanent kind is **time**; the permanent kind is **magnitude** (*miqdār*). Magnitude divisible in only one direction is a **line**; in two directions a **surface**; and in three a **mathematical body** (*jism taʿlīmī*). A line is a single extension allowing separation only in one direction. Line, surface and body are continuous quantities: the supposed parts of a line meet at a common point, those of a surface at a common line, and those of a body at a common surface. Similarly, when time is thought divided, an instant (*ān*) is imagined as the limit of the past and the beginning of the future. By contrast, if **five** is divided into two and three, there is no common boundary between those numbers. If one of the five is designated as the common boundary, only four members remain in the collection; if a further member is introduced, the collection has become six.

**On the words, “And it is peculiar to.”** A mathematical body can be conceived on condition that nothing else accompany it; proponents of a contrary view have even held that such an entity could exist separately outside the mind. Imagining a line without attending to surfaces or anything else gives a mathematical line.

If divisibility belongs to something of itself, it is intrinsically quantified—like number, time and magnitude. Intrinsic quantity does **not** admit intensity and remission: a number is not *more intensely numerical* than another, nor a magnitude *more intensely a magnitude*. Increase and decrease differ from many and few in that either of the former pair is understood only through reference to the other; multitude and paucity need not be conceived in this expressly correlative way. Intrinsic quantity likewise admits no true contrariety. Numbers cannot have maximum opposition between them and cannot exist as two contrary accidents in one subject: one number is included in another. Magnitudes likewise admit neither maximum opposition nor the relevant unity of subject; each magnitude may serve as a recipient of another or be received by it.

**On the words, “There is no inconsistency.”** The same thing may be intrinsically quantified in one respect and derivatively quantified in another. **Time**, intrinsically a continuous quantity whose parts do not remain together, may also be spoken of as a discrete, stable quantity through its relation to motion and to the spatial magnitude across which motion extends. Likewise a thing can be quantified derivatively in several ways. **Motion** is derivative quantity insofar as it inheres in the subject of a quantity, the moving body: hence its divisibility, for the movement of half the moving body is half that of the whole. Again, motion corresponds to the continuous quantity of the traversed distance, and so can be greater or less: movement to the midpoint is less than movement to the end. Finally, it corresponds to time, a nonpermanent continuous quantity, and accordingly differs in speed and slowness: a given distance is traversed faster in one time-unit than in two. Conversely, discrete quantity can belong to a continuous quantity, whether nonpermanent or permanent: “this day contains ten hours,” “this cubit comprises six handbreadths.”

**On the words, “Magnitude is sometimes taken.”** “Length,” “breadth” and “depth” may each mean **extension itself**, in the respects discussed above; then they are pure quantities. But length can also mean the first dimension posited, the longer of two dimensions, the dimension from a human head to feet or animal head to tail, or a radius from the centre of a sphere to its circumference. Taken in these ways, the terms are no longer pure quantities: they include relations or comparisons. title: Do numbers, magnitudes, lines and surfaces exist as accidents?
en:
### Do numbers, magnitudes, lines and surfaces exist as accidents?

**On the words, “The theologians denied.”** The theologians' denial of the existence of quantities in general is well known. Their treatment of **number** follows what was said in the chapter on unity and multitude and appears to rest on their denial of mental existence. Otherwise, philosophers do not count number among independent external entities either, but among intellectual considerations. The objection to **time** will be treated presently. As for **magnitudes**, the theologians build their denial on the proposition that bodies are assembled from indivisible atoms, aggregated through **contact** without the complete continuity that removes boundaries and divisions. The atoms arranged along a single direction constitute what is called a line, and by consideration of this arrangement the aggregate is called long. Atoms arranged in two directions constitute a surface, and in this respect the aggregate is said to have breadth. Differences in dimension depend upon the smaller or greater number of constituent atoms.

Even if magnitudes are not substances, the theologians argue that they are **privative**: surface is the termination or interruption of the body, line the termination of a surface, and point the termination of a line. They do not recognize a separately existent “mathematical body.” Even if these termini did exist, what is supposedly constituted from privations would itself be privative.

The philosophers defend the claim that magnitudes are accidents, not substantial parts of a body, in a general and in a more detailed way. **Generally**, magnitudes change while the numerically identical body remains. A particular lump of wax may be shaped as a sphere with one continuous surface and no lines, then as a cube with several surfaces and edges. The cube itself may be stretched into a rectangle, with greater length and less breadth, then reshaped the other way round. The body remains, but its magnitudes change.

**In detail**, the possession of a surface by a body depends upon the body's being **finite**, since an infinite body cannot be bounded by a surface. But the body's finitude requires an argument, to be given in the treatment of finite dimensions. If surface were part of the very substance of body, the existence of the surface would not be dependent on that separately demonstrated property. Likewise a sphere's possession of a line may depend upon its rotating about itself, thereby determining two stationary points, its poles, between which lies the axis, and an equatorial great circle upon its circumference. Alternatively, a line may arise through cutting a sphere, producing a circular surface bounded by a circular line. Whatever belongs to a thing through something else cannot be the thing itself or a part of its essence.

They further contend that magnitudes are **positive existents**, since they have determinate positions at which we can point and say, “here”; no such sensory indication can be directed toward sheer nonexistence. At most, the surface belongs to the mathematical body, line to surface and point to line **in virtue of a termination**: the cessation of extension in a certain direction. This privative condition does not make the conditioned quantity nonexistent. A positive entity can be conditioned by and qualified through what is privative.

**The theologians reply:** what changes while the body remains is the positional arrangement of its indivisible atoms, which can join or separate and possess specific configurations of conjunction or separation. If this is all that is meant by magnitudes, there is no dispute. But if the claim is that magnitudes are further accidents inhering in bodies, distinct from their atoms and the arrangements of those atoms, it is denied; nothing stated proves it unless the existence of indivisible atoms has first been refuted. Likewise the alleged dependence of line and surface on something outside body and its constitutive requirements merely restates the contested issue. On our view lines and surfaces are the indivisible atoms themselves **in a particular arrangement**—in one direction without breadth, or in length and breadth without depth. What is contingent upon something else is that **particular configuration**, not a further independent magnitude. And as for sensory indication of something positioned, what we point to is the atoms arranged in a certain manner. The alleged termini are absences and interruptions: beyond those atoms there are no further atoms.

title: Investigation 2: Time — arguments against its existence (I–II)
en:
### Investigation 2: Time — arguments against its existence (I–II)

**On the words, “The second investigation, concerning time.”** The theologians have offered a number of arguments for denying time's positive existence.

**First argument: an infinite regress of times.** If time existed, some of its parts would precede others. It is certain that time is not something whose constituent parts remain together, as though an event occurring now were also occurring on the day of the Flood. Rather, if it exists, it is a continually passing and disappearing thing, with one part arising after another **temporally**. The earlier and later cannot coexist here, though they may coexist in other kinds of priority. Time itself would therefore have to stand within another time, in which its parts are earlier and later; and the same question would recur without end.

**Reply:** it is necessarily known that some parts of time are prior to others **by their own nature**, without coexisting—as yesterday precedes today simply through their meanings, without any additional attribute. If one chooses to call this “temporal priority,” no difficulty arises. If one insists that each earlier and later thing must itself occur *within another time*, the standard list of five kinds of priority is incomplete: priority among the parts of time constitutes a **sixth kind**, suitably called priority in virtue of the thing itself.

**Second argument: no past, future, or present time exists.** Time is either past, future or present. Past and future are nonexistent; so, it is argued, is the present. Were the present existent, it would be either divisible—which is impossible, since time's parts cannot coexist—or indivisible. On the second alternative, one may turn to the next portion which becomes present, and so on: time is composed of successive indivisible instants. Yet time corresponds to motion, motion to the traversed distance, and distance is a magnitude belonging to a body. This would require a body to be constituted of indivisibles, an inadmissible consequence on the philosophers' assumptions (and something the theologians may support independently with appropriate arguments).

**Objection by way of counterexample:** the same argument would prove that **motion does not exist**. Its past and future parts do not exist, while an indivisible present would imply indivisible parts of motion—yet motion's existence is evident. **The theologians reply:** that counterexample does not confute us dialectically, because we ourselves acknowledge indivisible parts. Nor does it refute our argument independently, for what exists of motion is the moving body's **continuously obtaining an intermediate position** between the beginning and end of its path; this is not itself divisible into past, future and present in the way alleged. Time, by contrast, is intrinsically divisible quantity and is not something simultaneously obtained all the way from beginning to end. Plainly, what occurred on the day of the Flood is not occurring now. The discussion of motion will examine this distinction further.

**Answer to the original argument:** we do not grant that past and future time are absolutely nonexistent. “Past” means precisely what has passed away **after having been**, and “future” what is about to be. At most, neither exists **at the present moment**. **Objection:** the past is neither now nor in the future, nor could it have existed in the past: when it existed, it must have been divisible (in which case time's parts would coexist) or indivisible (which entails the indivisible part). The future is subject to the same difficulty.

**Reply:** “existent in one of the times” is a narrower predicate than “existent absolutely.” The falsity of the narrower predicate does not entail the falsity of the broader. **Objection:** but the existent is a universal exhausted by what exists in the past, present or future. If every class into which a universal is exhaustively divided is nonexistent, the universal is nonexistent too, for it exists only in one of its instances. **Answer:** we deny that what exists must fall under those three predicates. There may be things whose existence bears no temporal relation and so which exist **without existing in any time**—time itself could be such a thing. Motion, by contrast, exists only in time. Hence Avicenna says that an endless succession of past motions does not produce a series of *simultaneously existing* infinitely numerous things: if past motions were currently existent, they would have to be existent in the past, present or future in the disputed sense, and each alternative would be impossible.

One may grant that time itself falls under past and future—and, if there is a present, under the present too; but the present is not a third temporally extended region, merely the **common limit** of past and future. Each of the two can be existent **in some respect** although neither is existent *in one of the three temporal regions*. The impossibility of this requires proof.

**Objection:** what exists in this general way must still be either divisible, making the parts coexist, or indivisible, yielding an indivisible atom of time. **Answer:** if divisible, there is no coexisting, since **coexistence means simultaneous presence**, the absence of a part's being preceded by another; merely being divisible does not entail it. Or, if called indivisible, this need not entail an indivisible part: there can be **possible division in imagination** without actual division. This response can also be directed against the second argument from the outset.

title: Time: the third argument against it and the philosophers' proofs
en:
### Time: the third argument against it and the philosophers' proofs

**Third theologian argument.** If time existed, it could not subsequently cease to exist. For the “after” in “nonexistence after existence” would have to be temporal: this is not the priority of one part of time to another, since the later nonexistence is plainly not essential to the earlier time in that way. Another time would therefore be required for the passage into nonexistence. If time cannot cease, it must be **necessary of existence**, which is impossible for something composite, divisible, successive and constantly perishing in its parts. The Necessary Existent has none of these properties.

**Answer:** nonexistence *after* existence need not be **in another time**. It could obtain at the instant which is the limit of the time that has passed, namely the boundary at which that time terminated. Even conceding the necessity of temporal description, the impossibility of time's cessation does not make time intrinsically necessary. At most it would be perpetually existent through the continual succession of its parts. Nothing impossible follows simply from that.

**On the words, “And they established it.”** The philosophers defend time's positive existence with several arguments.

**First: the varying capacity for traversing a distance.** Consider one movement over a fixed distance at a specified speed and another at that same speed. If they agree both in beginning and in ending—they start together and stop together—they necessarily traverse the same distance. If they agree in stopping but the second began later than the first, the second necessarily traverses less. Likewise, if they agree in beginning and ending but the second is slower, it traverses less. Between the first rapid movement's beginning and cessation there is the possibility of traversing a determinate distance at a determinate speed, and of traversing less at a given slower speed; while between the later rapid movement's beginning and cessation the possibility of traversing the first distance at the fixed speed is smaller. There is therefore something **quantitative**, intrinsically admitting more and less, within which movement occurs and according to whose magnitude movement differs. Such variations must ultimately depend on something intrinsically quantitative, not merely on something quantitatively described in virtue of another. This is the measurable possibility just described, and we call it **time**. Therefore time exists.

This magnitude of possibility cannot simply be the **speed**, **extension of the traversed path**, or **extent of the moving body**. These can vary independently of the quantity of time: one whole movement might be equal to half another in speed while differing in total extent; movements can cover equal distances in unequal times through differing speed, or cover different distances in equal times. A fast mover may traverse a parasang in an hour while a slow one traverses half a parasang in that hour. A small and a large body may traverse the same path within an hour; equally sized bodies may traverse that path in one hour and half an hour respectively. The quantity under investigation is therefore not reducible to one of these others.

**Objection:** the proof employs the very temporal predicates whose external existence is in dispute: that two motions are simultaneous or successive, that one is faster—traversing the path in less time or more distance in equal time. title: Aristotle's definition of time and objections to it (I–III)
en:
### Aristotle's definition of time and objections to it (I–III)

The ways of **measuring recurring events** thus differ with what the speaker believes the hearer will recognize. Ordinary people say “sit for a day”; to someone who recites, “for as long as it takes to read al-Fātiḥa”; to a writer, “for the writing of a page”; and to a Turk, “for the cooking of a pot of meat.” Such usages plainly do not disclose the **essence of time**; they merely identify occasions by known events.

Aristotle and his followers, among the philosophers, instead hold that **time is the magnitude of the motion of the outermost sphere**. They argue: time is a magnitude, that is, continuous quantity. It is quantitative because it admits equality and inequality: the time of one revolution equals that of another, is less than that of two revolutions, and greater than that of half a revolution. It is continuous because, were it discrete, it would terminate in absolutely indivisible constituents like the units of number—discreteness being precisely of that kind. Time would then be constituted from successive indivisible instants, requiring indivisible segments of movement and of distance because time corresponds to motion and motion to distance. Further, time is the measure of something **whose parts do not persist together**, namely motion. If it measured a permanent whole, time itself would have its parts simultaneously existing, so that what happens today would happen on the day of the Flood—impossible.

This nonpermanent magnitude cannot be that of a **straight-line motion**. Every such motion must cease, since dimensions are finite and consecutive straight motions cannot continue endlessly on a finite path, as will be explained. Time, however, does not cease, as argued. It must therefore be measured by a **circular motion**. The movement must be the fastest one, so that its measure is the shortest and can measure all other movements. A smaller unit measures a greater whole, not conversely—for example, cubits measure a parasang and tens measure a hundred. The fastest motion is the daily revolution assigned to the outermost celestial sphere. Time is therefore the magnitude of this motion.

**Objection:** this is a *definition* of time disclosing its essential constituents; how can these be established by proof? **Reply:** where a thing is conceived only under a partial description rather than apprehended in its essence, argument may establish the constituent elements of its real nature. Thus philosophers seek proofs for the soul's substantiality or the body's composition from matter and form. Here all that we initially conceive is something in virtue of which things are described as earlier and later. Being quantitative is not essential to this initial *description*, though on the theory it is essential to the reality described.

**Critique of the argument:** it rests upon disputed theses—denial of indivisible particles, the impossibility of connecting motions without intervening rest, the necessary pause between successive linear movements, and the impossibility of time's annihilation, together with the claim that its cessation would require a further time. Even if these are demonstrated, or conceded by a philosophical opponent so that the argument is addressed only to other philosophers, we do not accept that anything admitting degrees must thereby be an independently existing **quantity**. That would follow only if the differing degrees belonged to it essentially, which is precisely what is disputed; a bare assertion of necessity cannot establish this.

**On the words, “Then it was opposed.”** The cited theory receives several counterarguments.

**First**, if time were a magnitude of **motion**, stable or permanent realities could not properly be said to be *in* time. For time would then be changing and nonpermanent—indeed the measure of change should itself be changeable—and a changing thing cannot correspond point by point to an unchanging thing. Such correspondence requires that earlier and later parts in one be matched in order with earlier and later parts in another. But we are as certain that **rest**, the heavens and other enduring realities, even the Necessary Existent and all separate entities, exist “yesterday, today and tomorrow” as we are that movement occurs at those times. Denying the former seems no less arbitrary than denying the latter.

The same reasoning was used against Abū al-Barakāt's assertion that anything persistent can be thought to persist only within continuous time; what remains existent must have a temporal magnitude for its persistence, even when it is not supposed to be in time. Consequently, he identifies time as **the magnitude of existence**. But if that magnitude itself changes, it cannot be mapped onto the unchanging, and if it is stable, it cannot be mapped onto the changing.

**Second**, “motion” has two meanings, as will be explained. One is the mobile thing's **being between the beginning and the end** of its trajectory, a continuously existing condition in the relevant sense. The other is the extended passage through the distance from beginning to end, a purely imaginary whole which does not exist outside the mind, since its parts are never settled together. If time measures motion in the first sense, it must itself be a stable, nonflowing quantity, which is impossible. If it measures motion in the second sense, time is not existent, since a positive existent cannot inhere in a nonexistent thing.

**Third**, if time were the measure of the outer sphere's motion, imagining time to exist without that motion would be inconceivable. Yet we are certain that an ongoing, passing reality in virtue of which things are past and future, before and after, would obtain even if no sphere or movement existed. Suppose a duration during which the sphere did not exist and then came into existence; or during which it rested and then moved; or during which its movement or the sphere itself came to an end. Such suppositions do not resemble the contradictory attempt to conceive an actual motion as not occurring *while it is occurring*. If we can deny time in the absence of motion, we can deny it just as well in its presence, and conversely; the alleged conceptual dependence has not been shown.

title: Time, eternity (*dahr*) and everlastingness (*sarmad*); continuing replies
en:
### Time, eternity (*dahr*) and everlastingness (*sarmad*); continuing replies

The disappearance of time when the outer sphere's motion disappears is plainly not self-evident in the way that the removal of a thing's magnitude follows the removal of the thing. This is why no rational investigator has taken the supposed beginninglessness and endlessness of the celestial spheres as self-evident. It also shows that time cannot simply **be the outermost sphere itself or its motion**, as certain thinkers suppose.

**Replies to the three objections** have nevertheless been attempted. Against the first it is said that an existent is properly *in* time only if it changes—either actually, possessing earlier and later, past and future, beginning and ending, as motion and moving things do, or hypothetically, as **rest** does. To say that a thing rests “for an hour” means that, if motion occurred in place of the rest, that motion would last an hour. Avicenna says that saying “the body is in time” means that it is involved in motion, while motion is in time. What remains stable in itself, by contrast, is described as existing **with time**, not **in time**. It does not have a part corresponding to the earlier portion of time and another part corresponding to its later portion. Thus the continuous stability of heaven can be conceived as **with** the continuous stability of earth, without one existing *in* the other. There is no doubt that motion being together with time, heaven being together with time, and heaven being together with earth are different determinate senses of togetherness, for which language may supply different expressions.

Thus it has been said that the relation of **changing to changing** is *zamān* (time); that of **stable to changing** is *dahr* (eternity or perduring time); and that of **stable to stable** is *sarmad* (everlastingness). Both kinds are embraced by unrestricted **duration** (*dawām*); the past without a beginning is *azal*, and futurity without end is *abad*.

The Imām replies that this is impressive-sounding language without a definite account. The meaning of “was” and “will be,” if it is an external existent, must be either changing, in which case it cannot correspond to the stable, or stable, in which case it cannot correspond to the changing. Merely changing words does not resolve the dilemma. **Objection to the Imām:** correspondence between the changing and the stable is not impossible. We say “So-and-so lived for a thousand years,” thus comparing the duration of one continued existence to a thousand solar revolutions. Theologians themselves say that the Eternal exists in indefinitely many **supposed times**. **Answer:** then the original claim fails that time, because it is nonpermanent, cannot measure an abiding or permanent condition. Moreover, the duration of life corresponding to a thousand revolutions is an instance of changing matched to changing: the *duration* is time, and the revolution is motion.

Strictly, time is not itself merely the **relation**: it is the changing reality **to which another changing reality is related**. Nor do these philosophers mean just any relation but a relation of *togetherness*, as some state explicitly. They have, however, explained this togetherness chiefly by saying that it is not the togetherness of two things both occurring within a single time. As for things other than motion, a moving thing is related to time by existing **with** it, not **in** it. When the togetherness is that of the stable with the nonstable, they call it *dahr*; of the stable with the stable, *sarmad*. This existence-with corresponds, in the case of stable things, to the existence-in-time of temporal things; it is, as it were, a “when” (*matā*) for abiding things. But neither *dahr* nor *sarmad* should be imagined as extended: otherwise it would be a magnitude of motion.

They go further: time is as though an **effect of dahr**, and dahr as though an **effect of sarmad**. Were the relation of corporeal causes to their principles not permanent, the bodies could not exist, still less their motions; and if time's relation to the principle of time were not permanent, time itself would not occur. Avicenna accordingly says: considering the states of changing things with respect to changing things gives **time**; considering stable things with respect to changing things gives **dahr**, and considering stable things with respect to stable things gives **sarmad**. *Dahr* in itself belongs to *sarmad* but, as considered against time, is *dahr*: it is in itself stable, receiving its name through reference to time, which is changing. This is what we have found in explanations of the statement. Its lack of a determinate, satisfactory meaning is nonetheless apparent, as the Imām maintains.

**Reply to the second objection**—the distinction between the mobile's stable intermediate condition and its imagined complete trajectory. We choose the movement of **traversing** (*qaṭʿ*) as the motion whose magnitude is time. It is nonpermanent: one portion of it exists after another without two portions being simultaneously actual. That **successive arising and perishing** is precisely its mode of extramental existence. Only the complete imagined movement from starting point to endpoint is not actual as a finished totality. Its magnitude, time, is the same: the whole viewed at once is imaginary, but it arises and passes continually, with portion after portion coming to exist. This is the force of saying that something nondivisible in actuality produces time **through its flow**, just as a body's being at an intermediate position yields the act of traversing through its ongoing succession.

**Objection:** this seems to involve a train of successive indivisible instants, since the alleged nondivisible flowing element can only be the instant (*ān*). The answer begins by distinguishing **actual parts** from the **potential partition** of a continuous quantity: time is continuous and admits division through supposition and imagination, without consisting of already detached parts.

title: The actuality of time; Rāzī's objections; the ancient view of time as substance
en:
### The actuality of time; Rāzī's objections; the ancient view of time as substance

The defender completes the preceding reply by saying that time possesses no actual detached parts, but admits division merely in supposition and imagination. **The Imām objects:** on that account time seems not to exist at all. The complete extension is imaginary; its supposed parts are nonexistent; what, then, is the alleged actual constituent of time? Distance is different: its parts may be divided only in imagination, but the **continuous whole** which admits imagined division exists outside the mind. Motion is also different insofar as there is an actually continuous state of **being between the endpoints**, and no contradiction arises from its existence.

**Further reply:** the mind conceives an extension which is not itself an extramental whole, but such that, were it to be posited and divided, its supposed parts would exhibit successive, perishing relations of earlier and later. Such an extension can arise in the mind only if there is outside it a nonpermanent, changing reality whose continuity of occurrence and nonstability generate this conceived extension. If that extension is divided in supposition, its supposed parts are prior and posterior **by their own nature**, without requiring another time. Motion's correspondence to time is accounted for in the same way. Since the two parts do not exist together except in conception, the priority and posteriority which relate them also exist only in conception. This is why such relations can also be ascribed to **number**. If earlier and later were actual extramental **correlatives**, the relata would have to coexist, forcing time's past and future portions to exist together and making time permanent. The assertion that “what exists outside the mind of time bears priority and posteriority” is thus metaphorical: the real changing occurrence is **that by reason of which** these relations obtain between the imagined parts of the mentally extended time, not an extramental substratum literally carrying the two relational accidents.

This is the most precise formulation offered in response to the Imām's objections: if the priority of nonexistence before an event required time, why not yesterday's priority to tomorrow, or motion's simultaneity with time? If priority and posteriority were positive extramental correlatives, how could even **nonexistence** be called earlier or later? Would they themselves occur in time, producing regress? And how could their substrates avoid simultaneous existence if both were actual correlatives? If instead they were intellectual considerations without external being, why should their presence indicate an extramental time? title: Investigation 3: Place — surface, dimension and void
en:
### Investigation 3: Place — surface, dimension and void

**On the words, “The third investigation, on place.”** There is no doubt of the actuality of something **from which a body passes and in which it rests**, or which does not admit another body together with it. This is what is named **place** (*makān*). The serious philosophical positions differ over its nature. One identifies it as the **inner surface of the surrounding body**, contiguous with the outer surface of what it contains: Aristotle and his Peripatetic followers adopt this account. A second identifies place with **extension or dimension** (*buʿd*) into which the body's own extension penetrates and with which it becomes united; many philosophers and theologians adopt versions of this view.

The advocates of dimensional place distinguish two kinds of dimension. The first is **material extension**, inhering in a body and subsisting through it, such that another extension of the same kind cannot coexist with it as an additional attribute of that body. This is what is called the **mathematical body**. The second is **separate extension**, not subsisting in a receptacle; instead a body occupies it completely, while the body's own dimension coincides and becomes united with it. According to the theologians, this separate extension is sheer nonbeing, a simple absence capable of remaining without any occupant: the imagined **empty space** which would be empty were nothing to occupy it. According to certain philosophers, by contrast, it is a **positive extension** of a cubit or some smaller or larger length, large enough to receive this body or one smaller or larger.

For clarification, imagine a vessel emptied of water, air and everything else. Between its extremities is an extension which could be occupied by water or air, and an extension also seems to be there when it is filled. This has been called the **naturally apprehended extension** (*al-buʿd al-mafṭūr*), because it is supposedly manifest to innate understanding: everyone judges that water is *between the vessel's boundaries*. Another explanation of the name is that the extension admits or “opens” to an entering body with its dimensional magnitude. Plato is reported as sometimes calling it **matter**, since bodies successively enter it as forms come to matter, and sometimes **form**, because it is the dimensions extended in different directions, like the corporeal form of continuity whereby a body admits dimensions and is distinguished from separate entities. Under this second interpretation one cannot object that no rational person could identify a body's spatial region with a constituent of that very body, since it is evident that the body's *place* is not a part of it.

On the position attributed to Plato and his followers, this separate extension **cannot be empty of an occupant**; some others allow it to be empty. Those who affirm **void** (*khalāʾ*) therefore include the theologians and certain philosophers. Two principal questions must be treated: first, whether place is a **surface** or a **dimension**; second, whether **void is possible**.

**First question: Arguments that place is a surface.** The proponents begin by claiming that place can only be dimension or surface, and dimension is impossible.

**Their first argument against dimension:** dimensional place must either be **imagined or merely supposed**, as theologians say, or **actually existing**, as Plato and others say. The first is impossible because place exists—either self-evidently or through arguments: places are equal or unequal, since we can say that one place equals, exceeds, or is less than another by a half, third, quarter, or some other amount; we can point to one place with sense and say a body moves from it to another; we describe places as small, large, long, short, near, far, contiguous or separate. Sheer absence admits none of these predicates.

The second alternative is also rejected. If positively existing dimensional place itself admits local motion from one place to another, **it must itself have a place**, which will require another place, and so on without end. This is the impossible regress of places previously discussed. Since, by hypothesis, all the indefinitely numerous places are dimensions, all would admit motion and require a place. Their encompassing place would have to be **inside** the totality, because it is one of those places, yet **outside** it, because it encompasses them. Contradiction. If, on the other hand, dimensional place does not admit local motion, then the body inhering in or inseparably conjoined to it should not admit motion either, since its inseparable concomitant would possess a determination excluding motion. What necessarily accompanies a thing cannot be incompatible with the thing's own possibility of moving.

**Their second argument:** if place is positively existing extension, placing a body in a place means **interpenetrating two magnitudes**: the extension inhering in the body penetrates the extension which is its place. But a vessel full of water clearly contains only one extension; two identical extensions would be present in one subject.

title: Place as dimension: further criticisms and arguments in its favour
en:
### Place as dimension: further criticisms and arguments in its favour

It would also force doubt upon immediately apprehended facts—for instance, that a certain extension is **one cubit** long. Perhaps it is really two or more cubits which are interpenetrating. It would likewise cast doubt upon the equality in magnitude of an occupying body and its place: perhaps one extension is larger and, through their interpenetration, produces only the magnitude we observe. Both consequences are universally rejected.

**Third argument against dimensional place:** extension considered in itself must either depend upon a receptacle, in which case it cannot be separated from matter as the theorists of independent spatial extension require, or it is independent of a receptacle, in which case it could not inhere in matter, as bodily magnitude does. For an accident's inherence in a receptacle means its determination to and dependence upon that receptacle for its constitution. The suggestion that something can be independent of a receptacle in its essence and yet happen to inhere in one does not evade this argument as it stands.

**Answer to all three objections:** the magnitude inherent in a body may be **different in quiddity** from the separate extension constituting place, while sharing with it an essential or accidental feature, “extension” in general. The former may therefore be specially disposed to motion and require a receptacle, while the latter allows other magnitudes to penetrate or occupy it. Their conjunction would not be the coincidence of two identical accidents in a single subject. Moreover, the very picture of “two magnitudes in one occupying body” is inaccurate: one magnitude inheres **in the occupied body**, while the other is the extension **within which that body is located**.

**On the words, “The proof for extension.”** Those who identify place with extension argue that, if it were merely a **surface**, a number of things which reason immediately affirms would become false.

One is the **equality of a place's magnitude with that of what occupies it**. Take a rounded ball of wax and flatten it into a thin sheet. Its enclosing surface becomes several times greater, though the amount of wax remains the same. Round the sheet again: its surface contracts while its material remains unchanged. Similarly, hollowing a deep cavity in a cube can enlarge the surrounding surface while reducing the body's amount. If place were the surrounding surface, it would change in magnitude independently of the body accommodated.

Another is that **every body is in a place**. But the body surrounding everything is not itself enclosed by a further body whose internal surface could be its place. Again, a bird hovering motionless in the air during a strong wind is at rest, although the surfaces of the surrounding air continually change. Yet a change of place either is spatial motion or necessarily entails it. Conversely, the moon's circular motion is movement even though the enclosing surface of its own celestial sphere remains the same; unchanging place should entail rest, since changing place is either movement or its necessary concomitant.

Further, the **place from which Zayd departed** is said to remain, although air has now filled it, and the former surface enclosing Zayd is no longer there. Every interior **part of a body** has its own spatial region, yet internal parts of water, for example, do not directly touch an air-surface; one can say they are “in the air” only derivatively, just as one says “water is within the celestial sphere.” We also judge a body to be **here or there** without first deciding whether some other body encloses it. We can conceive a solitary body touched by nothing else, but cannot conceive a body occupying **no spatial region**. Finally, we judge that the northern and southern poles of the sphere are located in **different regions** and that each point on the surface of the enclosing celestial sphere moves with it from place to place.

These considerations and others strongly incline judgement toward **dimension** rather than **surface** as the nature of place, though there remains room to dispute whether some alleged consequences are really impossible, or whether they follow from the rival theory.

**Second question: Is void possible?** The dispute concerns **an empty expanse with nothing occupying it**, whether that is called extension or not and whether it is understood as a positive reality or a purely imagined absence. **Objection:** how can someone who calls void sheer negation, something without any actual being, affirm its *possibility*? **Answer:** it means that two bodies could be so situated that they **do not touch one another** and that there is **no third body between them touching them**.

Those who allow void give several arguments. **The first** imagines two equally smooth flat plates, one laid exactly on the other with their level surfaces in contact and no body between them. Raise one plate from the other **all at once**: at the first moment of its elevation the intervening region must be empty, since air arriving from outside would first have to pass around the edges before filling the centre. The argument relies on premises its opponents are assumed to accept: the possibility of perfectly smooth flat surfaces without protrusions, depressions or merely juxtaposed atomic parts; contact of whole surfaces rather than merely of their indivisible constituents; simultaneous raising of the entire top plate rather than lifting one side before the other; and the absence of air newly created in the centre or admitted through microscopic interstices between atomic parts. **Reply:** we deny that the upper plate can be lifted in this precisely specified fashion at all, for its raising would entail the impossible. Even if lifting it is possible in a general way, it does not follow that... [argument continues].

title: Arguments for the possibility of void: separation, displacement and experiment
en:
### Arguments for the possibility of void: separation, displacement and experiment

The response to the two perfectly smooth plates continues. If “all at once” means **at an indivisible instant**, we deny that the specified raising is possible, since elevation is motion and requires time. If it means only that all the parts begin to move together, to prevent the plate's bending or separation, we deny that a void follows: the motion occupies a period during which air can pass from the edges to the centre. The defender of void must therefore establish **both** that this exact separation is possible and that it necessitates an empty intervening region. The opponent may deny either premise. If instead one merely assumes the instantaneous **loss of contact** between the two surfaces, intending to force the view that separation itself is momentary, the decisive reply is to deny that such instantaneous loss of contact is possible in the way proposed.

**Second argument: displacement would be impossible without void.** If there were no void, a body could not move from one place to another. When it enters a new place, the body previously occupying that place either perishes and another body appears in the region left behind by the first mover, or it does not. The first is contradicted by your own admissions and by reason in many cases, as in the movement of all the small components of a rotating wheel into successive positions. If the occupying body does not perish, it either remains where it is or leaves. If it remains and preserves its magnitude, the moving body must interpenetrate its material dimensions: two bodies would occupy one region, universally and evidently impossible. If it remains but becomes **denser or smaller**, thereby making room for the new body, that occurs either because it has matter capable of receiving different magnitudes—an affirmation of **prime matter** (*hayūlā*), said by the objectors to be demonstrably refuted—or because it comprises parts with empty interstices that close up during compaction. In the latter case void exists after all, contrary to the assumption that no void exists.

If the previous occupant moves away, it either enters the **first body's former place** or moves to a third place. In the former case the two movements allegedly form a circle of mutual dependence: each body's entering the other's place requires that other to leave first, since they cannot coexist there; yet each departure requires the other's entrance lest there be a void. In the latter case all bodies must displace their neighbours through a never-ending chain of movements; because the number of bodies is finite, this must ultimately return to the circular situation. Similar alternatives apply to the region **vacated** by the original moving body: it either remains empty, is filled by another arriving body, or is filled through rarefaction of neighbouring bodies, whether by changes of dimension in underlying matter or through opening up void between atoms.

Thus the mover's destination must be either a **genuine void**, or a body whose own empty interstices can be reduced by compression, allowing room for the newcomer. A fish's movement in water is said to be of this second kind; it therefore does not refute the argument.

**Answer:** the proof offered against prime matter is not conclusive, as will be explained; at most it raises objections to premises of arguments offered *for* matter, which cannot establish its impossibility. Even if the impossibility of matter is conceded, a supposed circle of displacement need not be vicious. If “each movement depends on another” means merely that neither occurs **without the other**, as in correlated events, we deny that this is impossible. The spokes or parts of a rotating wheel are precisely such a case. Each moves into the region of its predecessor only as the succeeding part changes place; otherwise either a gap or a separation would occur. But the succeeding part's movement also presupposes the first movement, to avoid two bodies occupying one place. This is a **circle of simultaneity** (*dawr al-maʿiyya*), not a circle of causal priority. If, instead, “depends” means that each movement has to be *causally preceded* by the other, the alleged conclusion is denied. The argument has not established a **circle of prior causation** (*dawr al-taqaddum*). It can also be questioned whether rarefaction and condensation presuppose either real prime matter or pre-existing void interstices at all.

**Third argument:** if void did not exist, every bodily surface would have to touch another bodily surface, without end. For the existence of void is precisely the possibility of a body not touching another. Since bodies are finite in the aggregate, the required infinite succession of enclosing surfaces is impossible. **Answer:** the inference is denied. Bodies can terminate at an outer surface with **nothing whatsoever beyond it**. Simple nonexistence outside the world is not an **empty interval capable of being occupied**, which is the void under dispute.

**Fourth argument: apparently observable voids.** Several experiments are cited. (a) If the air is sucked forcefully out of a flask and the flask is inverted into water, water rises into it. It is argued that the flask must have become empty; were it still filled, water could no more enter than it could before suction. (b) Press the two sides of a flexible waterskin together, expel the air, and seal its neck and pores tightly with pitch. If the sides are pulled apart, there will be void inside. (c) Inflate a sealed waterskin as fully as possible, then drive a needle or several needles into it. Their easy entrance is taken to reveal empty space already inside, for otherwise they could not enter without bodily interpenetration. (d) Transfer the contents of a full wine-cask to a waterskin, then insert the filled waterskin into the same cask: if both fit, the liquid must originally have contained gaps of void equivalent to the waterskin's volume.

**Replies:** none necessitates void. A small quantity of air may remain in the flask and become rarefied under suction; when suction ends it returns toward its natural volume, drawing in water because an empty space is impossible. Some air may remain between the pressed sides of the waterskin and expand when they are separated, or external air may enter through tiny pores despite careful sealing. The needles can enter an inflated skin through condensation of the air or by expelling some of it through pores. In the cask, the liquid may condense, or a small amount may evaporate or otherwise become rarefied under pressure in a manner sufficient to account for the waterskin's displacement. These are physical alternatives; the alleged experiments do not by themselves compel acceptance of void.

The response to the two perfectly smooth plates continues. If “all at once” means at an indivisible instant, we deny that the specified raising is possible, since elevation is motion and requires time. If it means only that all the parts begin to move together, to prevent the plate's bending or separation, we deny that a void follows: the motion occupies a period during which air can pass from the edges to the centre. The defender of void must therefore establish both that this exact separation is possible and that it necessitates an empty intervening region. The opponent may deny either premise. If instead one merely assumes the instantaneous loss of contact between the two surfaces, intending to force the view that separation itself is momentary, the decisive reply is to deny that such instantaneous loss of contact is possible in the way proposed.

Second argument: displacement would be impossible without void. If there were no void, a body could not move from one place to another. When it enters a new place, the body previously occupying that place either perishes and another body appears in the region left behind by the first mover, or it does not. The first is contradicted by your own admissions and by reason in many cases, as in the movement of all the small components of a rotating wheel into successive positions. If the occupying body does not perish, it either remains where it is or leaves. If it remains and preserves its magnitude, the moving body must interpenetrate its material dimensions: two bodies would occupy one region, universally and evidently impossible. If it remains but becomes denser or smaller, thereby making room for the new body, that occurs either because it has matter capable of receiving different magnitudes—an affirmation of prime matter (hayūlā), said by the objectors to be demonstrably refuted—or because it comprises parts with empty interstices that close up during compaction. In the latter case void exists after all, contrary to the assumption that no void exists.

If the previous occupant moves away, it either enters the first body's former place or moves to a third place. In the former case the two movements allegedly form a circle of mutual dependence: each body's entering the other's place requires that other to leave first, since they cannot coexist there; yet each departure requires the other's entrance lest there be a void. In the latter case all bodies must displace their neighbours through a never-ending chain of movements; because the number of bodies is finite, this must ultimately return to the circular situation. Similar alternatives apply to the region vacated by the original moving body: it either remains empty, is filled by another arriving body, or is filled through rarefaction of neighbouring bodies, whether by changes of dimension in underlying matter or through opening up void between atoms.

Thus the mover's destination must be either a genuine void, or a body whose own empty interstices can be reduced by compression, allowing room for the newcomer. A fish's movement in water is said to be of this second kind; it therefore does not refute the argument.

Answer: the proof offered against prime matter is not conclusive, as will be explained; at most it raises objections to premises of arguments offered for matter, which cannot establish its impossibility. Even if the impossibility of matter is conceded, a supposed circle of displacement need not be vicious. If “each movement depends on another” means merely that neither occurs without the other, as in correlated events, we deny that this is impossible. The spokes or parts of a rotating wheel are precisely such a case. Each moves into the region of its predecessor only as the succeeding part changes place; otherwise either a gap or a separation would occur. But the succeeding part's movement also presupposes the first movement, to avoid two bodies occupying one place. This is a circle of simultaneity (dawr al-maʿiyya), not a circle of causal priority. If, instead, “depends” means that each movement has to be causally preceded by the other, the alleged conclusion is denied. The argument has not established a circle of prior causation (dawr al-taqaddum). It can also be questioned whether rarefaction and condensation presuppose either real prime matter or pre-existing void interstices at all.

Third argument: if void did not exist, every bodily surface would have to touch another bodily surface, without end. For the existence of void is precisely the possibility of a body not touching another. Since bodies are finite in the aggregate, the required infinite succession of enclosing surfaces is impossible. Answer: the inference is denied. Bodies can terminate at an outer surface with nothing whatsoever beyond it. Simple nonexistence outside the world is not an empty interval capable of being occupied, which is the void under dispute.

Fourth argument: apparently observable voids. Several experiments are cited. (a) If the air is sucked forcefully out of a flask and the flask is inverted into water, water rises into it. It is argued that the flask must have become empty; were it still filled, water could no more enter than it could before suction. (b) Press the two sides of a flexible waterskin together, expel the air, and seal its neck and pores tightly with pitch. If the sides are pulled apart, there will be void inside. (c) Inflate a sealed waterskin as fully as possible, then drive a needle or several needles into it. Their easy entrance is taken to reveal empty space already inside, for otherwise they could not enter without bodily interpenetration. (d) Transfer the contents of a full wine-cask to a waterskin, then insert the filled waterskin into the same cask: if both fit, the liquid must originally have contained gaps of void equivalent to the waterskin's volume.

Replies: none necessitates void. A small quantity of air may remain in the flask and become rarefied under suction; when suction ends it returns toward its natural volume, drawing in water because an empty space is impossible. Some air may remain between the pressed sides of the waterskin and expand when they are separated, or external air may enter through tiny pores despite careful sealing. The needles can enter an inflated skin through condensation of the air or by expelling some of it through pores. In the cask, the liquid may condense, or a small amount may evaporate or otherwise become rarefied under pressure in a manner sufficient to account for the waterskin's displacement. These are physical alternatives; the alleged experiments do not by themselves compel acceptance of void.

title: Arguments that void is impossible; the resistance argument and its replies
en:
### Arguments that void is impossible; the resistance argument and its replies

**On the words, “The proof of impossibility.”** Those who deny void—that is, a region such that two bodies neither touch each other nor have a third touching body between them, but leave an interval capable of occupancy, whether positive or privative—give several arguments.

**First: motion without resistance would take the same time as motion with resistance.** That consequence is manifestly false, so void must be impossible. Suppose a body travels one parasang through void. It must do so in time; let it take one hour. Now suppose that **the same body under the same motive force** travels one parasang through a plenum. Because of resistance it must take more time; let it take two hours. Then imagine a less dense plenum whose density is proportioned to the times in void and in the first plenum—half as dense as the first. The journey through this less resistant medium would allegedly take one hour: with distance, mover and motive force equal, greater or lesser speed, measured by greater or lesser time, follows solely from greater or lesser resistance. We have thus made the time of movement in a resisting medium equal to the time of movement without any resisting medium—an unacceptable result.

Several objections are offered. **First**, we deny that a plenum of any arbitrarily required density is possible. The density of a medium might have a lower limit beyond which no thinner medium exists. **Second**, we deny that resistance is divided in the same proportion as density: halving the density need not halve the resistance, unless it is shown that resistance is a force distributed through the material and divided with it, requiring no minimal density to obtain. **Third**, we deny that resistance cannot become so weak that its presence makes **no difference** compared with its absence.

**Fourth—and this is the most significant objection**, since the others might be answered especially on philosophical assumptions—the proportionality of the resisting media does not imply the alleged proportionality of total travel times. That would follow only if **every part of the time required were due to resistance**. But movement itself may demand a certain duration even without resistance, such as the hour already posited in void. In the thinner resisting medium, one hour is attributable to the movement as such, just as in void, and a further half-hour is attributable to resistance at half the former strength, since a stronger resistance had added an hour. The total would be **one and a half hours**, not the one hour alleged by the proof.

This objection is due to **Abū al-Barakāt**. His language in *al-Muʿtabar* suggests that the interaction of a given motive force with a given moving body **demands a determinate duration** for the motion even in the absence of a medium that must be pierced. Resistance, if present, adds to this duration: part of the time is thus assigned to overcoming the medium and part to the movement without that medium—the time of its hypothetical passage through void. The base duration varies with the mover's force and the moving body's properties. By “the motion itself” he means **this particular body's motion under this particular force**, abstracting from the resistance of an intervening medium, not the universal quiddity of motion considered simply as motion.

One might object that, if the quiddity of motion as such demanded a fixed duration, every instance would require that duration, since an effect cannot fail to follow the nature which necessitates it, whereas a particular motion could occur within a fraction of the supposed duration. But that objection misses the specific meaning of “motion itself” just explained. Nor does Abū al-Barakāt mean a movement **stripped of all degrees of speed and slowness**, which some investigators argue is impossible. Every motion must traverse some distance during some time, each indefinitely divisible. Imagine another traversing the same distance in half as long: the first is slower; imagine one taking twice as long: the first is faster. Motion wholly free of speed and slowness is therefore said never to occur, and what cannot occur can demand no duration.

Two difficulties arise for this last reasoning. A motion's duration may be indivisible except in imagination; motion within a physically impossible portion of that duration would then be impossible. That an impossibility implies other impossibilities does not establish that a faster or slower motion **could actually occur**. Mere hypothetical comparison cannot prove slowness in the first movement or disprove its being the fastest possible. **Objection:** even if slowness is not established, speed must be, for another movement in a **longer** time is plainly possible. Hence motion devoid of speed and slowness cannot exist. **Reply:** the particular response against Abū al-Barakāt depends on establishing **slowness**, so that time is assigned to resistance; mere reference to speed is a correlative supplement. This is why *al-Mawāqif* expresses the reply in the form: “If motion required a duration of itself, motion taking that duration would be the fastest of all motions,” as explained earlier.

The investigating philosopher's thought can also be phrased differently: motion necessarily exists with a determination of speed or slowness, which are themselves due to resistance; thus there is no motion without resistance, so any time required by motion is also, indirectly, a time associated with resistance, even if resistance contributes nothing to **motion's own demand for time**. On this interpretation one cannot object that the necessary coexistence of speed and slowness with motion is consistent with the motion's having a duration in its own right; nor does the analogy of essential properties that always occur with accidental qualifications refute the position. It still does not rebut **Abū al-Barakāt's objection**, however, or prove the investigator's claim that motion of itself demands no time.

**Second argument: a body would have no reason to occupy this part of a void rather than another.** Void, if conceived as sheer negation or as perfectly homogeneous extension, contains no intrinsic differentiating factors. Choosing one location would therefore be a preference without a determining reason (*tarjīḥ bilā murajjiḥ*). **Answer:** even granting that all portions of void are alike, the claim does not follow for the world as a whole if void is finite, since the world would occupy all its parts. With indefinitely extended void, or for particular bodies, an **extrinsic reason** may determine location: a voluntary agent's will, or the intrinsic tendency of some bodies to surround the whole and of others to be nearer to or farther from its encompassing boundary.

**Third argument: a thrown stone would reach heaven.** If the region between earth and heaven were empty, a stone thrown upward would continue all the way to the heavens, since the thrower has imparted an upward-moving force that the stone's natural tendency cannot overcome except with the assistance of collisions with the filled medium. **Answer:** besides presupposing the denial of a freely acting agent, the argument at most excludes a **purely empty region throughout the interval between earth and heaven**. It does not exclude void outside that interval or empty regions interspersed among portions of air.

**Fourth argument: observable phenomena would not occur if void were possible.** Such phenomena include flesh rising inside a cupping vessel during suction: the withdrawn air is followed by the flesh to avoid empty space; water rising through a tube when one end is immersed in water and the other sucked; water remaining inside a pot with a narrow opening in its bottom when the pot's upper mouth is sealed, instead of flowing out and leaving an empty region, and flowing out when the top is opened to admit air; and a closed flask whose neck is tightly fitted with a wooden plug. Remove the plug and the flask breaks **inward**, allegedly to prevent the plug's region becoming empty; push the plug in and the flask breaks **outward**, since the interior is filled and its occupant cannot coexist with the wood.

**Answer:** the phenomena may have **other causes**. At most, these arguments establish that the phenomena would follow **if void were absent**. The consequent can obtain for other reasons; affirming it does not establish the antecedent. Such observations may perhaps furnish **immediate intuitive assurance** (*yaqīn ḥadsī*) to an individual observer, but they do not amount to a compelling demonstration against a disputant.

**End of Chapter 2: quantity, time and place.**

title: Chapter 3: Quality — definition, four classes and sensible qualities
en:
### Chapter 3: Quality — definition, four classes and sensible qualities

**On the words, “The third chapter, on quality.”** The highest genera cannot be defined through complete essential definitions; at most one can provide imperfect descriptive definitions (*rusūm nāqiṣa*). They have no higher genus, as is obvious. Nor can we simply posit differentiae, since the idea that two constituents of equal rank might compose a thing, each functioning as a differentia, is a mere logical possibility, whose actual occurrence is unknown and perhaps demonstrably impossible. For quality (*kayf*), the only known universal concomitant is that it is accidental and distinct from both quantity and relational accidents. A definition through these terms, however, would explain something through notions no clearer than itself: none of the highest genera is naturally more evident than another.

The philosophers therefore replace “quantity” and “relational accident” with their clearer distinctive features. A quality is **an accident which of itself does not require division, and the conception of which is not dependent upon first conceiving something else**. This excludes substance, quantity and relational accidents. Those who treat point and unity as accidents add that quality must also **not require indivisibility**, so as to exclude those two. The words “of itself” and “primarily” qualify both the absence of a required division and the absence of a required indivisibility, lest **knowledge of a composite** or **knowledge of a simple** be excluded merely because its object is composite or simple. **Objection:** some qualities, such as knowledge, power, straightness and curvature, necessarily involve conceiving some other thing. **Answer:** this is an implication or consequence, not the dependence of their first conception on a prior conceived term. Conceiving them entails conceiving some object, whereas a relative notion cannot be conceived until the two terms related have first been conceived. If anything conventionally placed among qualities fails to meet the intended criteria, it is not a quality in the requisite sense.

A familiar definition calls quality **an abiding disposition** whose conception does not necessitate the conception of anything external to it and its subject, and which entails neither division nor relation among its subject's parts. The last qualification excludes position (*waḍʿ*); “abiding” is supposed to exclude time, acting and being-acted-upon. Critics observe that acting and being-acted-upon are already excluded by the requirement concerning an external term, and time by absence of division. Moreover some qualities, like **sound**, are nonabiding, while others, like knowledge and power, do implicate another object in their conception.

**On the words, “It is exhausted, by induction, in four classes.”** The usual four are: **sensible qualities** (*kayfiyyāt maḥsūsa*), **qualities of soul** (*nafsāniyya*), **qualities peculiar to quantities**, and **dispositions or capacities** (*istiʿdādāt*). This enumeration rests upon **induction**. A classification phrased as successive affirmative and negative alternatives may provide different verbal schemes, but they amount to saying “if quality is class one, it is class one; if two, two; if three, three; otherwise four.” Such schemes cannot demonstrate exhaustiveness and are at best ways to arrange cases already known through induction. Even their criteria are sometimes obscure or too narrow. Thus the Imām describes psychic qualities by the notion of **perfection**, while Avicenna describes them as unrelated to bodies and dispositions as attached to body qua natural. Sensible qualities are sometimes characterized by **their activity**, and more narrowly by producing a likeness of themselves in another: heat warms a neighbour and blackness projects its image into the eye. But **heaviness** moves a body rather than making it heavy; the Imām rightly notes that this apparent definition excludes heaviness and lightness although Avicenna elsewhere in *al-Shifāʾ* explicitly includes them among sensible qualities. In another place Avicenna admits it has not been demonstrated that moist things make other things moist and dry things make them dry.

Likewise, to define qualities belonging to quantities as qualities associated with **body qua quantity** loses the qualities belonging specifically to **number**, since number may be conceived without an external material body. This relates to the objection that mathematics is said to treat what is separable from matter mentally but not externally, even though mathematics includes number, which can be separated from matter externally too. One reply distinguishes number considered without reference to material dependence—unity and plurality as treated in metaphysics—from arithmetical operations of addition, subtraction and multiplication considered in material applications. That reply is disputable. Nor can we simply say “body in some respect,” so that numerical qualities are included, for then the opposite criterion for psychic qualities—“not related to body”—would mean absolutely no bodily association. This is clearly false. The intended meaning is rather that psychic qualities are **not exclusively bodily in a way independent of soul**.

**First class: sensible qualities.** If a sensible quality is relatively firmly established—such as gold's yellow colour or honey's sweetness—it is called a **passive quality** (*kayfiyya infiʿāliyya*), either because the senses undergo an affection from it, or because, in that particular instance or generally, it follows from a mixture (*mizāj*) produced by the mutual affections of the elements and their matters. Particular dependence appears in a compound such as honey's sweetness; general dependence is found in elemental heat, since heat as a kind may arise in a mixed body through an interaction of its material constituents. That is the meaning of the philosopher's reference to the quality's **individualization or its species**. There is no separate additional species “heat of fire” distinct from other heat, nor “whiteness of snow” distinct from the whiteness of ivory, in the literal or relational way sometimes suggested. If a quality is not firmly settled, it is called a **passion** (*infiʿāl*): its rapid disappearance makes it especially akin to something presently undergoing affection, and the name distinguishes it from the firmly established kind.

title: Fundamental tactile qualities: heat, cold, moisture and dryness
en:
### Fundamental tactile qualities: heat, cold, moisture and dryness

**First investigation: the primary tangible qualities.** These are the qualities of which no elemental body is devoid, whether or not they are actually being sensed: **heat, cold, moisture and dryness**. Their existence is obvious. The suggestion that cold is merely the absence of heat is without merit. Their essences are likewise already apprehended, so attempted definitions merely draw attention to characteristic properties rather than generate the primary concepts themselves.

A familiar property ascribed to **heat** is that it separates unlike things and joins like things. This is, however, secondary to a more fundamental property, **motion upward**. A definition attributed to the philosophical tradition describes heat as “an active quality which moves what bears it upward,” by imparting lightness, with the incidental consequence that it collects homogeneous things and separates heterogeneous things. By dissolving dense material it produces **rarefaction in the qualitative sense**, a thinning of consistency, whose opposite is **condensation** understood as thickening. By raising subtle material it may produce **condensation in the positional sense**, the coming together of like material particles as foreign components are removed. This contrasts with “rarefaction” as loosening and expansion of particles so that another body enters their intervals. The word “active” means **producing a likeness of its own quality in something else**, not merely producing any effect whatever.
